svg.title: A VRF is four objects on one device, and it exists only on the PE
svg.desc: One PE drawn as a box containing two VRFs, red and blue, each with its own routing table, its own interface set, its own RD and its own RT policy. Four numbered parts explain what a VRF is made of: an independent routing table, the interface list bound to it, an RD that makes its routes globally unique, and RT import and export rules that decide which routes may enter. A right panel shows what a VRF is not: it is not a VLAN, it is not encryption, and it does not exist on the CE or on the P router. A closing note explains that the same physical PE can carry two customers with the same 10.0.0.0/8 prefix and that the isolation holds only because the two tables never meet.
svg.text: A VRF is four objects, and all four must be right for isolation to hold
Get any one of them wrong and the symptom looks like a routing bug somewhere else
PE1 — one box, two customers, one prefix
1. Routing table. Independent RIB, and a separate FIB partition.
2. Interface membership. Each interface belongs to exactly one VRF.
3. RD. Makes this VRF's prefixes globally unique in VPNv4.
4. RT import / export. Decides which routes may enter and leave.
Miss 2: an interface sits in the global table and answers global routing.
Miss 3: two VRFs with the same RD collide in the VPNv4 table.
Miss 4: the route arrives but is not imported, which looks like no route at all.
The first two fail loudly. The last two fail by silence.
Not a VLAN (layer 2, one broadcast domain). Not encryption.
Not present on the CE, and not present on the P router at all.
Same prefix in two VRFs, then ping across: it must fail.
If it succeeds, one interface is in the wrong table.
The mental model worth keeping: a VRF is a router inside a router. Everything you know about routing still applies inside it — adjacencies,
metrics, summarization — and nothing crosses between two VRFs unless a route target explicitly allows it. That “unless” is the whole design.
Operational note: always read the routing table with the VRF name attached. A missing “vrf” keyword on the command is the most common false diagnosis in L3VPN support.
